title: Advil or Tylenol for a Hangover? Which Is Safer After Drinking
excerpt: Advil or Tylenol for a hangover? How ibuprofen and acetaminophen differ after drinking, which one to choose for your situation, safe timing and doses, and when to skip both.
metaDescription: Advil or Tylenol for a hangover? Which is safer after drinking, which works better for a hangover headache, safe timing and doses, and when to skip both.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** for a healthy adult who drank a normal amount and has no stomach, kidney, or liver problems, either Advil (ibuprofen) or Tylenol (acetaminophen) at a single label dose the next morning is a reasonable choice. Most people who are hungover are better served by **Advil, taken with food and water, once the alcohol has cleared.** It is easier on the liver, and hangover headaches seem to involve inflammation, which ibuprofen targets and acetaminophen mostly does not. Tylenol becomes the better pick if you have a sensitive stomach, a history of ulcers, kidney problems, or take a blood thinner. Neither one is a good idea if you drink heavily every day, and neither should be taken "in advance" before bed.

**The quick rules:**

- **Wait until the alcohol is out of your system.** Don't take either one while drinking or right before bed after a big night.
- **Eat something and drink water first.** This matters most for Advil, which can irritate the stomach.
- **Take the lowest dose that helps.** One or two 200 mg Advil tablets, or one or two 500 mg Tylenol caplets. Not both stacked on top of each other "for extra strength."
- **Check your other medicines.** Acetaminophen hides in NyQuil, DayQuil, Excedrin, and many cold and sleep products. Ibuprofen and naproxen (Aleve) shouldn't be combined.
- **If you have 3 or more drinks most days,** talk to a doctor or pharmacist before using either one. Both labels carry an alcohol warning at that exact threshold.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and the official label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and the medicines you take. **Talk to a doctor or pharmacist before using either painkiller after drinking if** you drink 3 or more drinks most days, have liver disease or high liver enzymes, have had a stomach ulcer or bleeding, have kidney disease or heart disease, take a blood thinner, steroid, or blood pressure medicine, are over 60, or are pregnant. **Get emergency help (call 911, or Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 in the US) if** you may have taken more than the labeled dose, you vomit blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, you have black or tarry stools, severe stomach pain, yellow skin or eyes, confusion, or you can't keep fluids down.

## Advil vs Tylenol at a Glance

They are both over-the-counter pain relievers, but they work in different ways and put the strain on different parts of your body. That difference is the whole decision.

| | Advil (ibuprofen) | Tylenol (acetaminophen) |
|---|---|---|
| Drug type | NSAID (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug) | Pain and fever reliever, not an anti-inflammatory |
| Fights inflammation? | Yes | Very little |
| Main risk with alcohol | Stomach irritation and bleeding; kidney strain when dehydrated | Liver injury, especially with high doses or regular heavy drinking |
| Label alcohol warning | Stomach bleeding risk if you have 3 or more drinks every day | Severe liver damage risk if you have 3 or more drinks every day |
| Take with food? | Yes, strongly recommended | Helpful, not essential for the stomach |
| Usual single adult dose | 200 to 400 mg (1 to 2 tablets) | 500 to 1,000 mg (1 to 2 Extra Strength caplets) |
| OTC daily ceiling on the label | 1,200 mg (6 tablets) in 24 hours unless a doctor says otherwise | 3,000 mg (6 Extra Strength caplets) on the Tylenol Extra Strength label; 4,000 mg is the absolute upper limit for healthy adults |
| Better pick if you have... | Liver concerns (but ask your doctor if you have liver disease) | Stomach ulcers, reflux, kidney problems, or take blood thinners |
| Hidden in other products? | Some combination cold and sinus products | Very often: cold, flu, sleep, and combination headache products |

For the full detail on each drug, see our deep dives on [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) and [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol). This page is the head-to-head: which one to reach for, and when to skip both.

## Why the Choice Matters After Drinking

On an ordinary day, the difference between Advil and Tylenol is mostly about which one works better for your kind of pain. After a night of drinking, it's also about which organ is already under stress.

Alcohol affects your body in several ways that overlap with how these painkillers can cause harm:

- **It irritates the stomach lining.** Alcohol increases stomach acid and can inflame the lining of the stomach. That's part of why you feel queasy the morning after. Ibuprofen also weakens the stomach's protective layer, so the two add up.
- **It dehydrates you.** Alcohol suppresses a hormone (vasopressin, sometimes called antidiuretic hormone) that tells your kidneys to hold on to water, so you urinate more. NSAIDs like ibuprofen reduce blood flow to the kidneys a little, which normally doesn't matter, but can matter more when you're low on fluids.
- **It is processed by the liver.** Your liver handles alcohol first. Acetaminophen is also broken down in the liver, and a small slice of each dose becomes a toxic by-product the liver has to neutralize. Regular heavy drinking makes that harder.

So the real question isn't "which painkiller is stronger?" It's "which part of my body can best handle a little extra work this morning?" For most healthy people after a normal night out, the answer is that both can handle a single label dose. For some people, the answer clearly points one way.

## How Advil Works, and Its Risks With Alcohol

Ibuprofen blocks enzymes called COX-1 and COX-2. These enzymes make prostaglandins, chemical signals involved in pain, swelling, and fever. Blocking them reduces pain and inflammation.

The trouble is that some prostaglandins have a protective job. In the stomach, they help maintain the mucus layer that shields the lining from acid. In the kidneys, they help keep blood flowing, especially when you're dehydrated. Reduce them, and both organs lose a little protection.

**Stomach.** The US label for ibuprofen warns that the chance of stomach bleeding is higher if you have 3 or more alcoholic drinks every day while using the product, take it longer than directed, take more than directed, are 60 or older, have had stomach ulcers or bleeding, or take a blood thinner or steroid. For a social drinker taking one or two tablets with breakfast, the risk is low. For someone who drinks most days and takes ibuprofen often, it is meaningfully higher.

**Kidneys.** Short-term, normal doses of ibuprofen are generally not a problem for healthy kidneys. The concern is mostly for people who are significantly dehydrated, older, or already have kidney disease or heart failure, or who take certain blood pressure medicines (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or diuretics). A rough morning after with vomiting and very little to drink is a time to rehydrate before reaching for an NSAID.

**Liver.** Ibuprofen is processed by the liver but rarely causes liver problems at normal doses. This is its main advantage over Tylenol after drinking. One important exception: people with advanced liver disease such as cirrhosis are usually told to avoid NSAIDs because of bleeding and kidney risks. If you have any liver condition, ask your doctor which pain reliever is right for you.

## How Tylenol Works, and Its Risks With Alcohol

Acetaminophen relieves pain and fever, but scientists still aren't completely sure how. It seems to act mainly in the brain and spinal cord rather than at the site of pain, and it has very little anti-inflammatory effect. That's why it's gentle on the stomach: it doesn't strip away the protective prostaglandins in the stomach lining the way ibuprofen does.

Its weak spot is the liver. Most of each dose is safely processed and removed in urine. A small share is turned by a liver enzyme (called CYP2E1) into a toxic compound called NAPQI. Your liver normally neutralizes NAPQI right away using an antioxidant called glutathione. Problems start when NAPQI is made faster than glutathione can clean it up.

Regular heavy drinking pushes on both sides of that balance. It increases the amount of the enzyme that makes NAPQI, and it lowers glutathione stores, especially when combined with poor eating. Fasting lowers glutathione too. That's why the US label warns of severe liver damage if you have 3 or more alcoholic drinks every day while using acetaminophen, and why acetaminophen is a leading cause of acute liver failure in the United States, much of it from accidental overdose.

For one person taking one normal dose the morning after a single night of moderate drinking, the risk is low. Short clinical studies of normal doses in drinkers have generally not found meaningful liver harm. The danger lives at the edges: too many pills, too many days, hidden acetaminophen in other products, little food, and a pattern of heavy drinking. Our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) walks through the liver chemistry and safe timing in detail.

## Which Works Better for a Hangover Headache?

Here's the honest part: **there are no good head-to-head trials of Advil versus Tylenol for hangovers.** Systematic reviews of hangover treatments, including a well-known review in the *BMJ* in 2005, found no compelling evidence that any common remedy reliably treats or prevents hangovers. Painkillers mostly help with one symptom, the headache, and don't touch nausea, fatigue, or the foggy, run-down feeling.

That said, there's a reasonable case that an anti-inflammatory like ibuprofen fits the hangover headache a little better:

- **Hangovers appear to involve inflammation.** Research in alcohol and clinical pharmacology has found that levels of inflammatory signaling molecules (cytokines) rise after heavy drinking and appear to track with how bad people feel the next day. Prostaglandins, the signals ibuprofen blocks, are part of that inflammatory picture.
- **An older small trial pointed the same way.** A small study from the early 1980s tested tolfenamic acid, an NSAID related to ibuprofen that isn't sold in the US, and reported fewer hangover symptoms compared with placebo. It was small and old, so treat it as a hint, not proof.
- **Acetaminophen doesn't target inflammation.** It can still dull a headache, but it doesn't address the inflammatory component.

So in theory, ibuprofen has a slight edge for the typical throbbing hangover headache, and many people report that it works better for them. In practice, both can take the edge off, and the safety picture for *you* matters more than the small possible difference in effect. If your stomach is already upset, the "better" headache drug may simply make you feel worse.

For more ways to ease a pounding head without leaning on pills, see our guide to [fast relief for hangover headaches](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025).

## Which One Should You Take? A Simple Decision Guide

Use this as a starting point, not a substitute for a pharmacist's advice. If more than one line applies to you, the more cautious one wins.

**Reach for Advil (ibuprofen) if:**

- You're a healthy adult who drank a normal amount last night
- You can eat something with it and drink water
- You don't have a history of ulcers, stomach bleeding, or kidney problems
- You aren't taking blood thinners, steroids, or blood pressure medicines that affect the kidneys
- You want to avoid adding work to your liver

**Reach for Tylenol (acetaminophen) instead if:**

- You have a sensitive stomach, reflux, or a past ulcer
- Your stomach is already upset or you can't keep food down (though if you're vomiting repeatedly, focus on fluids and see the warning section below)
- You have kidney problems or heart failure
- You take a blood thinner such as warfarin, apixaban, or rivaroxaban, or daily aspirin for your heart
- You're over 60 and worried about stomach bleeding
- You haven't taken any other product containing acetaminophen in the last day

**Skip both and call a doctor or pharmacist first if:**

- You drink 3 or more drinks most days, or you've been binge drinking for several days in a row
- You have liver disease, hepatitis, fatty liver, or have been told your liver enzymes are high
- You have both stomach and liver concerns
- You're pregnant (acetaminophen is often the default in pregnancy, but this is a conversation for your doctor, and the FDA advises avoiding NSAIDs from about 20 weeks onward unless a doctor recommends them)
- You've already taken painkillers in the last few hours and aren't sure how much

## Should You Take Them Together or Alternate?

Combining ibuprofen and acetaminophen is a common medical approach for some types of pain, because they work in different ways. There's even an FDA-approved combination product, Advil Dual Action, that contains both.

For a hangover, though, combining them is usually unnecessary. A hangover headache in most people responds to one drug at a normal dose, plus water, food, and rest. Taking both means you take on both sets of risks: the stomach and kidney load from ibuprofen and the liver load from acetaminophen, on a morning when your body is already dealing with alcohol's after-effects.

If you do use a combination product, count it toward *both* daily limits. A dose of Advil Dual Action contains acetaminophen, so don't take Tylenol on top of it. And don't build a "stack" of several products, which is one of the most common ways people accidentally overdose on acetaminophen.

## What About Aspirin, Aleve, or Excedrin?

People often ask about the other painkillers in the cabinet. Here's how they compare after drinking:

- **Aspirin** is also an NSAID, and it's the hardest of the group on the stomach. It thins the blood for days after a single dose, which adds to bleeding risk when the stomach lining is already irritated by alcohol. It has the same "3 or more drinks every day" stomach bleeding warning. Most people are better off with ibuprofen than aspirin for a hangover.
- **Aleve (naproxen)** is an NSAID that lasts longer than ibuprofen, so one dose covers 8 to 12 hours. That long action also means a longer window of stomach exposure. Never take it together with Advil, since stacking NSAIDs multiplies the stomach risk without adding much relief.
- **Excedrin** combines acetaminophen, aspirin, and caffeine. It carries both the liver warning and the stomach bleeding warning, and the caffeine can make dehydration-related jitters or a racing heart feel worse. It's one of the most common hidden sources of acetaminophen, so if you take it, don't take Tylenol too.
- **Night-time versions** such as Advil PM and Tylenol PM add a sedating antihistamine (usually diphenhydramine). Alcohol is also a sedative. Don't take these the same night you've been drinking.

## Timing: Before Bed or the Next Morning?

One of the most common hangover myths is that you should take a painkiller before going to sleep to "get ahead" of the morning headache. This is a bad idea with either drug.

- **Before bed with Advil:** alcohol is still irritating your stomach, you probably aren't eating, and you're about to spend several hours without water. That's a poor setup for an NSAID.
- **Before bed with Tylenol:** you're adding work for your liver while it's still processing alcohol, often on an empty stomach, and before you even know whether you need it.
- **Either one, pre-emptively:** there's no good evidence that a bedtime painkiller prevents a hangover. You just take on the risk without a clear benefit.

The better approach is to wait. In the morning, drink a glass or two of water, eat something, and then decide whether you still need a painkiller. Often you need less than you think once you've rehydrated and eaten.

How long should you wait after drinking? There's no official number of hours that applies to everyone. The body clears roughly one standard drink per hour on average, but that varies a lot with body size, sex, food, and genetics. After a heavy night, alcohol can still be in your system well into the next morning. If you still feel drunk, it's too soon for either painkiller.

## Dosing Basics for the Morning After

These are general label figures for healthy adults, not personal advice. Always follow the label on your specific product, since strengths vary.

**Advil (ibuprofen 200 mg tablets):**

- Take 1 tablet with food and water. If that isn't enough, 2 tablets is the usual maximum single dose.
- Wait at least 4 to 6 hours between doses.
- Don't take more than 6 tablets (1,200 mg) in 24 hours unless a doctor tells you to.
- Don't take it for pain for more than 10 days without talking to a doctor.

**Tylenol Extra Strength (acetaminophen 500 mg caplets):**

- Take 2 caplets every 6 hours as needed.
- Don't take more than 6 caplets (3,000 mg) in 24 hours, per the Tylenol Extra Strength label.
- Count every other product you've taken that contains acetaminophen (look for "acetaminophen," "APAP," or "paracetamol" in the Drug Facts box).
- If you drink 3 or more drinks most days, ask a doctor before using it at all. Many clinicians suggest a lower daily ceiling for regular drinkers.

**More is not better with either.** Doubling a dose won't make a hangover headache go away faster. It just raises the risk.

## Warning Signs That Need a Doctor, Not a Painkiller

A hangover is unpleasant, but it should be getting better through the day, not worse. Some symptoms after drinking aren't a hangover at all, and a painkiller could hide them.

**Get emergency help (call 911) if someone:**

- Is confused, very hard to wake, or passes out
- Has slow or irregular breathing, or bluish or very pale skin
- Has a seizure
- Is vomiting repeatedly and can't keep any fluids down
- Has a sudden, severe "worst headache of my life," especially with a stiff neck, weakness, numbness, or trouble speaking

These can be signs of alcohol poisoning or another emergency, not a hangover.

**Call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) or get medical care if:**

- You or someone else may have taken more than the labeled amount of acetaminophen, even if they feel fine. Early acetaminophen poisoning often feels like nothing more than nausea and sweating, which is easy to mistake for a hangover. Treatment works best when started early.
- You took several products and aren't sure of the total.

**See a doctor promptly if, after taking ibuprofen or aspirin, you notice:**

- Vomit with blood or material that looks like coffee grounds
- Black, bloody, or tarry stools
- Stomach pain that doesn't get better
- Much less urine than usual, or swelling in your legs or feet

**See a doctor promptly if, after taking acetaminophen, you notice:**

- Pain under your right ribs
- Yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes
- Dark urine or pale stools
- Unusual tiredness, confusion, or easy bruising

**And if you find you need a painkiller after drinking most mornings,** or you get shaky, sweaty, or anxious when you haven't had a drink, that's worth raising with a doctor. Those can be signs that your body has started depending on alcohol, and suddenly stopping heavy drinking can be dangerous without medical support.

## What Actually Helps a Hangover (Besides Painkillers)

A painkiller treats one symptom for a few hours. The hangover itself fades as your body clears alcohol and its by-products, rehydrates, and recovers from a night of poor sleep. Things that genuinely help:

- **Water and electrolytes.** Rehydrating helps with headache, dizziness, and dry mouth. Plain water is fine; an electrolyte drink can help if you've been sweating or vomiting.
- **Food.** Simple carbohydrates like toast or crackers can help if your blood sugar is low and your stomach is unsettled. Food also protects your stomach if you take ibuprofen.
- **Sleep.** Alcohol disrupts deep and REM sleep, so part of the hangover is plain sleep deprivation. A nap genuinely helps.
- **Time.** There's no shortcut that makes a hangover disappear, despite what some products claim.

Prevention beats treatment. Drinking less, drinking more slowly, eating before and while you drink, and alternating alcoholic drinks with water reduce how bad the next morning feels. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

## Where Does DHM Fit In?

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that some people take when they drink. It's been studied mainly in animal and lab research for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver, with a small amount of human data. It's promising, but there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers reliably in people, and it doesn't replace sensible drinking.

Two things it is **not**: it's not a pain reliever, and it doesn't make it safe to combine acetaminophen or NSAIDs with heavy drinking. Follow the painkiller labels and alcohol warnings no matter what supplements you take. If you take prescription medicines, check our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) and ask your pharmacist.

If you want to try DHM as part of a sensible drinking routine, [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) is a popular option, and [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is a lower-cost choice. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

- For most healthy adults after a normal night out, **Advil with food and water** is the better first choice for a hangover headache. It spares the liver and targets inflammation.
- **Tylenol is the better choice** if you have stomach problems, kidney problems, or take a blood thinner, as long as you stay well under the daily limit and haven't taken other acetaminophen products.
- **Don't take either before bed** or while alcohol is still in your system. Wait, eat, hydrate, and then take one standard dose if you still need it.
- **Don't stack them** or combine multiple products without counting every ingredient.
- **If you drink 3 or more drinks most days, or have liver, stomach, or kidney conditions, talk to a doctor or pharmacist** before using either one after drinking.
- **If anything feels like more than a hangover,** get medical help rather than reaching for another pill.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is Advil or Tylenol better for a hangover?**

For most healthy adults, Advil (ibuprofen) taken with food and water once the alcohol has cleared is the better first choice. It's easier on the liver than Tylenol, and hangover headaches seem to involve inflammation, which ibuprofen targets. Tylenol is the better choice if you have a sensitive stomach, a past ulcer, kidney problems, or take a blood thinner. There are no good head-to-head trials, so safety for your situation matters more than the small possible difference in effect.

**Is it safe to take Advil after drinking?**

For most healthy adults, one standard dose (200 to 400 mg) the morning after a normal night out, taken with food and water, is unlikely to cause harm. Alcohol and ibuprofen both irritate the stomach, so the risk of stomach bleeding rises with heavy or daily drinking, higher doses, an empty stomach, age over 60, a history of ulcers, and blood thinners. If you have 3 or more drinks most days, ask a doctor or pharmacist first.

**Is it safe to take Tylenol after drinking?**

A single normal dose (500 to 1,000 mg) the morning after a few drinks is unlikely to harm the liver of a healthy adult who doesn't drink heavily day to day. The risk rises sharply with high or repeated doses, hidden acetaminophen in other products, not eating, and regular heavy drinking. The label warns that people who have 3 or more drinks every day should ask a doctor before using it.

**Can I take Advil and Tylenol together for a hangover?**

The two can be combined for some kinds of pain because they work differently, but for a hangover it's usually unnecessary. Combining them means taking on both the stomach and kidney risks of ibuprofen and the liver risk of acetaminophen. One drug at a normal dose, plus water, food, and rest, is enough for most people. If you use a combination product such as Advil Dual Action, don't add Tylenol on top, and count it toward both daily limits.

**Should I take a painkiller before bed to prevent a hangover?**

No. There's no good evidence that a bedtime painkiller prevents a hangover. Ibuprofen before bed can irritate a stomach that alcohol has already inflamed, and acetaminophen adds work for your liver while it's still processing alcohol. Wait until the morning, drink water, eat something, and then take a single dose if you still need it.

**How long should I wait after drinking to take Advil or Tylenol?**

There's no official waiting period that applies to everyone. Wait until the alcohol is out of your system (the body clears roughly one standard drink per hour on average, though this varies a lot), then eat and drink water before taking a standard dose. If you still feel drunk, it's too soon.

**Is aspirin better than Advil or Tylenol for a hangover?**

Usually not. Aspirin is the hardest of the common painkillers on the stomach and thins the blood, which adds to bleeding risk when alcohol has already irritated the stomach lining. Most people are better off with ibuprofen, or with acetaminophen if they have stomach concerns. Avoid Excedrin-type combinations unless you count the acetaminophen in them.

**What if I drink every day and need something for headaches?**

Talk to a doctor or pharmacist before using either one. Both the ibuprofen and acetaminophen labels warn specifically about people who have 3 or more drinks every day, because daily drinking raises the risk of stomach bleeding with NSAIDs and liver damage with acetaminophen. Needing a painkiller most mornings after drinking is also worth raising with a doctor in its own right.
